title: Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an observing capability that repeatedly resolves the ocean’s evolving three-dimensional temperature, salinity and absolute velocity across an entire basin, including deep and ice-covered waters. Here, synoptic means that measurements are sufficiently coordinated in space and time to distinguish evolving structures such as eddies, rather than assembling a picture from observations taken too far apart to resolve their evolution. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Electromagnetic remote sensing does not provide a weather-satellite view through the ocean interior. Sound can travel over long underwater distances, and acoustic travel times provide integral constraints on sound speed, temperature and currents. Recovering three-dimensional fields from those constraints requires inversion and often combination with other observations and circulation models. The innovation would therefore be a sustained observing and reconstruction capability, rather than a literal camera that directly photographs each interior location.

Proposed scope: success should be defined by the fields recovered, their resolution, coverage and independently validated uncertainty. Acoustic networks, profilers, moorings, mobile platforms or other suitable physics could contribute. A larger profiler array could be part of the solution if the combined system achieved the required performance; replacing existing networks is not itself the objective.

significance.text: Sustained basin-wide interior fields would substantially strengthen estimates of where the ocean stores heat and freshwater, how it transports them, and how circulation changes. Resolving mesoscale variability alongside deep and under-ice structure would connect observations across scales that present observing systems sample unevenly. The revolutionary consequence would be a much more tightly constrained account of the ocean’s evolving interior, including better estimates of absolute deep flow and better initial conditions for forecasts.

The satellite analogy describes the ambition for broad, repeated coverage, but has important limits. Interior observations already include profiles, moorings and acoustic measurements integrated over long paths; they are not exclusively isolated points. Synoptic sensing would strengthen inference rather than eliminate it: retrieval, inversion and assimilation would remain necessary. Complete heat and freshwater budgets would also require surface and boundary flux information, so interior fields alone would not guarantee budget closure.

Conditional downstream possibilities include better testing of ocean models, improved detection of changing storage and transport, and more informative forecast initialization. As a synthesis, these benefits depend on actual coverage, uncertainty and successful use of the observations. Even an excellent observing system would not by itself supply reliable centennial forecasts, a closed theory of turbulent transport or a prediction of overturning stability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central capability sought is sustained sampling and reconstruction sufficient to resolve evolving three-dimensional interior fields at basin scale. Acoustic thermometry and tomography establish useful physical foundations, but a long-path temperature constraint is not equivalent to a depth-resolved map of temperature, salinity and velocity. The supplied 2019 review describes a global multipurpose acoustic observing system as beginning implementation and recommends its development within GOOS; that historical assessment does not establish the system’s status in November 2026.

A fundamental retrieval barrier is separating the requested variables. Sound speed alone does not uniquely determine both temperature and salinity. Path-integrated observations also require enough independent information to distinguish vertical structure and horizontal variability, while current retrieval must resolve the flow information contained in acoustic propagation. A convincing solution must validate all three requested fields and their joint uncertainties, rather than treating successful thermometry as proof of complete interior sensing.

Acoustic approaches must also determine source and receiver positions and account for sound-speed variability through space and time. These quantities interact: uncertainty in propagation conditions affects positioning, while uncertain instrument locations complicate interpretation of travel times. Shared signals and joint estimation can help, but accurate navigation alone does not establish that the ocean fields have been recovered.

Engineering synthesis: the system would need adequate spatial geometry, repeated sampling fast enough to resolve the chosen phenomena, stable calibration, and sustained operation across deep and seasonally ice-covered regions. Coverage gaps and instrument drift would have to be propagated into field uncertainties. The unresolved question is whether an integrated system can maintain this performance over years and an entire basin, rather than only demonstrate individual measurements or selected paths.

current_state.text: The April 2025 OceanOPS report describes Core Argo as providing temperature and salinity profiles to 2,000 m at roughly 300 km spacing every 10 days, with enhanced sampling density in selected regions. This is a demonstrated, sustained profiling capability. Its nominal spacing and cycle do not by themselves establish the proposed basin-wide mesoscale fields, particularly below 2,000 m.

For Deep Argo, the report prepared for the GOOS OCG-16 meeting of 7–10 April 2025 described deployment as stalled at approximately 20% of global design. The April 2025 OceanOPS AST-26 report gave 17% implementation. These are dated reporting summaries, not interchangeable precision estimates: OceanOPS distinguishes implementation indicators involving activity, intensity, density and coverage. They should not be averaged or treated as a measured decline between two dates.

The U.S. Argo National Report to AST-26, dated 14 April 2025, records 219 operational Deep Argo floats globally in February 2025, including 124 U.S. floats. It also states that the SBE-61 sensor had not yet achieved its aspirational accuracy goals of ±0.001°C for temperature, ±0.002 psu for salinity and ±3 dbar for pressure, while reporting progress toward them. Those values are goals, not demonstrated accuracies. The supplied review found the count and sensor qualification explicit in the retained text despite PDF extraction warnings in this report; similar warnings in the OCG-16 report did not obscure its deployment statement.

Howe and colleagues’ peer-reviewed review, published on 26 July 2019, documents regional tomography demonstrations and ATOC’s role as a pilot for basin-scale ocean heat-content observation. It discusses combining integral acoustic observations with circulation models and recommends a complementary global multipurpose acoustic system within GOOS. ATOC therefore represents a demonstrated basin-scale thermometry foundation, not proof of all the proposed fields. Describing the history as a single pilot subsequently left unfinished would obscure the multiple demonstrations and broader implementation effort. The supplied review had a complete retained PDF for this assessment; truncation of a separate HTML capture did not limit these findings.

The research notes attribute useful measurements on instrumented paths to a 2023 seismic-ocean-thermometry paper and identify lower seismicity and a lack of suitable T-wave stations as obstacles to global application. They also attribute local ambient-sound thermometry at approximately 3 km scales, with accuracy below Argo’s, to a 2024 paper. Neither cited paper has a retained artifact in the supplied source index. Consequently, the supplied review could not verify the specific seismic limitation, the approximately 3 km result or the accuracy comparison. These remain qualified research-note reports, not established quantitative findings in this record; the missing evidence does not show that they are false.

The supplied evidence establishes dated profiling capabilities and historical acoustic demonstrations, but does not establish whether the complete proposed capability remained unachieved through 1 November 2026. The supplied freshness-search record is empty. A source retrieved in November 2026 can still describe conditions in 2019 or 2025; its retrieval date does not update those conditions. The concept remains a proposed performance objective here, with its cutoff-wide implementation status unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: recover sustained, depth-resolved temperature, salinity and absolute velocity fields over at least one ocean basin for several years, including depths below 2,000 m and a data-poor region such as the seasonally ice-covered Southern Ocean. The design should resolve both the seasonal cycle and mesoscale variability. Sustained coverage and under-ice observations are grounded in the documented observing goals, but this particular combination of requirements is a proposal, not an established community acceptance standard.
completion_criteria.label: Sustain basin-wide temperature, salinity and absolute velocity fields for years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: specify numerical spatial resolution, depth resolution, sampling cadence, acceptable outages and error targets before evaluating the demonstration. Validate each requested field against independent observations, including observations withheld from retrieval or assimilation. Report biases, calibration drift, joint retrieval uncertainties and the locations and periods where information is insufficient. Demonstrate resolution of evolving structures rather than relying on nominal instrument spacing or a model’s output grid.
completion_criteria.label: Validate evolving field resolution independently against prespecified numerical targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scientific success test: demonstrate a material reduction in uncertainty in basin heat and freshwater storage and transport estimates relative to a defined contemporary observing-system baseline. Account explicitly for surface and boundary flux uncertainties. Requiring the new estimates to differ from earlier estimates by more than the earlier error bars would be inappropriate: accurate agreement with substantially smaller uncertainty could itself be a successful result.
completion_criteria.label: Materially reduce basin storage and transport uncertainties against contemporary baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide sufficient observations, calibration information, retrieval methods and uncertainty procedures for independent teams to reproduce the principal results, and test performance across contrasting seasons, depths and circulation conditions. State operational demands and remaining coverage gaps. Any suitable physics and complementary observing networks may be used. A successful finite campaign would establish demonstrated breadth under its tested conditions; it would not establish global coverage or performance in every ocean regime.
completion_criteria.label: Make principal results independently reproducible and state operational limits

related_concepts.text: OCE-10, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, has a direct technical overlap: acoustic tomography and positioning can use the same signals and infrastructure, and precise positioning must account for four-dimensional sound-speed variability. Positioning can enable coherent sampling, while ocean observations can improve propagation estimates. The distinction remains the delivered capability: underwater locations do not by themselves constitute temperature, salinity and velocity fields. The supplied roster establishes the OCE-10 catalog identity.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-08, Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor, concerns seafloor displacement rather than ocean-interior fields. Acoustic implementations might share infrastructure or propagation corrections with interior sensing, but the supplied evidence does not establish this geodesy connection or its performance limitations. A benchmark network alone would not satisfy OCE-02, and a non-acoustic solution to either concept need not solve the other.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-01, A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport, and OCE-07, The stability class of the global overturning circulation, address explanation and prediction rather than observing coverage. Synoptic fields could constrain transport estimates and reveal evolving circulation, supporting tests of both concepts. Observation alone would not establish a turbulent closure or determine the overturning circulation’s stability class.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-04, Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth, could provide platforms for deep sampling and instrument support, while OCE-02 could supply environmental information useful to those operations. Persistent mobility is an operational capability; it does not guarantee basin-scale synoptic coverage. OCE-06, A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting, could benefit from better observations of surrounding ocean conditions, but verifying a melting law requires interface-specific evidence beyond basin interior fields.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-03, A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump, and OCE-09, A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer, could use better physical context for transport and environmental variability. Temperature, salinity and velocity fields would not supply the biological and biogeochemical mechanisms those concepts require. OCE-05, Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange, similarly concerns boundary exchange processes whose closure cannot be inferred from basin interior sensing alone. These remain separate innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved OCE-02 and its title while defining synoptic sensing as a sustained, validated field-reconstruction capability.
change_log.reason: The concept is scientifically meaningful even though individual supporting assertions and its November 2026 implementation status remain unresolved.

change_log.change: Replaced the points-only description of interior observations and the claim that inference would be eliminated.
change_log.reason: Existing acoustic measurements provide integral observations, and reconstruction would continue to require inversion or assimilation.

change_log.change: Added the temperature–salinity ambiguity, joint uncertainty requirements and coupling between positioning and sound-speed estimation.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why successful acoustic thermometry or navigation does not establish all requested fields.

change_log.change: Preserved the dated Argo quantities, clarified the global and U.S. float counts, and identified SBE-61 values as aspirational goals.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports these details while distinguishing implementation summaries and goals from achieved accuracy.

change_log.change: Reframed ATOC within multiple acoustic demonstrations and the 2019 global-system implementation effort.
change_log.reason: The earlier description oversimplified the history and could not establish subsequent noncompletion.

change_log.change: Retained the seismic and ambient-sound reports with explicit evidentiary qualifications.
change_log.reason: Their source artifacts are absent, leaving the claimed limitations, spatial scale and accuracy comparison unverified rather than disproved.

change_log.change: Replaced the requirement for changed budget estimates with a proposed uncertainty-reduction test.
change_log.reason: Improved observations can accurately agree with earlier estimates; complete budgets also require surface and boundary flux information.

change_log.change: Made resolution, independent validation, reproducibility and finite demonstration boundaries explicit.
change_log.reason: Nominal coverage or model output does not establish observed resolution, and proposed acceptance thresholds are not established standards.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to preserve related concept identities and separated supported technical overlap from roster-based synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster resolves the catalog assignments questioned in the review, but does not independently substantiate the proposed seafloor-geodesy connection.

change_log.change: Removed the cutoff-wide assertion of nonachievement and retained relevant extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: An empty freshness record cannot establish November 2026 implementation status; extraction warnings did not obscure the reviewed Argo passages.

unresolved_issues: Whether the complete proposed basin-field capability had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The specific seismic-ocean-thermometry limitation, approximately 3 km ambient-sound result and comparison with Argo accuracy require retained evidence from the cited papers.
Numerical resolution, cadence, uncertainty, coverage and operational acceptance targets remain to be defined for a concrete demonstration.
A contemporary baseline and a quantitative definition of material uncertainty reduction in storage and transport estimates remain unspecified.
The seafloor-geodesy overlap and its asserted sound-speed limitations remain plausible synthesis rather than findings established by the supplied evidence.

The review’s uncertainty about OCE-08 and OCE-10 catalog assignments was not retained because the supplied concept roster explicitly establishes those identities; the separate uncertainty about technical overlap remains.

brief.title: Repeated maps of the ocean beneath the surface
possible: People could follow changing temperatures, salt levels and currents throughout an ocean basin, including its depths and waters beneath ice. Repeated maps would capture moving swirls of water as they evolve, rather than piece together measurements taken too far apart.
why: Ocean scientists could track where heat and freshwater accumulate and how currents carry them. Better measurements of deep flow would help test ocean models and give forecasts a better starting point.

sources.who: S. Wijffels, B. King and B. Owens
sources.showed: Argo sustained its core observing network, while its deep-ocean network remained at roughly a fifth of its planned size.
sources.quote:
Deep Argo is stalled at 
~20% of global design.
sources.not_established: Network deployment does not establish repeated basin-wide maps of temperature, salt levels and currents.

sources.who: V. Turpin and O. P. de Fommervault, OceanOPS
sources.showed: Core Argo provides sustained temperature and salt measurements through the upper ocean. Its deep-ocean network is less complete.
sources.quote:
The Deep Argo mission, currently at 17% implementation, is advancing at a 
slower pace.
sources.cited_for: Existing floats provide sustained measurements but leave substantial deep-ocean gaps.
sources.not_established: Float spacing alone does not prove that maps can resolve evolving ocean structures.

sources.showed: Deep Argo floats operate in regional pilot networks. Sensor accuracy and stability remain under development.
sources.quote:
U.S. Deep Argo floats profile 
to pressures as great as 6000 dbar
sources.cited_for: Deep measurements are feasible, and regional networks already operate.
sources.not_established: Regional pilots do not establish sustained basin-wide coverage or achievement of sensor accuracy goals.

sources.showed: Their review describes regional mapping using sound and a basin-scale demonstration of measuring ocean heat through sound travel times.
sources.quote: that demonstrated and served as a pilot for a basin scale ocean heat content observing system (with cabled instrumentation)
sources.cited_for: Long-distance sound measurements provide a demonstrated foundation for observing ocean heat.
sources.not_established: Heat measurements along sound paths do not establish depth-resolved maps of temperature, salt levels and currents together.

sources.who: Authors of the earthquake-sound ocean temperature study
sources.showed: This is a study of measuring ocean temperature using sound from earthquakes.
sources.cited_for: Earthquake sound offers another approach to ocean temperature measurement.
sources.not_established: Measurements on instrumented paths do not establish complete basin-wide maps.

sources.who: Authors of the background-sound ocean temperature study
sources.showed: This is a study of measuring local ocean temperature using background sound.
sources.cited_for: Background sound offers an approach to local ocean temperature measurement.
sources.not_established: Local temperature measurement does not establish basin-wide coverage or recovery of salt levels and currents.

shown: Argo’s drifting instruments repeatedly measure temperature and salt levels down to 2,000 metres. Deep Argo extends measurements into deeper water through regional pilot networks.

Howe and colleagues describe experiments that used sound to measure regional ocean conditions and basin-scale heat changes. These establish useful foundations, but do not demonstrate the full mapping capability.
missing: A sustained system must recover temperature, salt levels and current speed and direction together throughout a basin, including deep and ice-covered waters.
Independent measurements must confirm that the maps resolve moving structures and accurately describe their own errors.
The system must maintain calibration, coverage and sufficiently frequent sampling over years.
Heat and freshwater estimates must become more precise while accounting for exchanges across the surface and basin boundaries.

milestones.label: Basin-wide maps sustained for years
milestones.explanation: Maps would have to track temperature, salt levels and current speed and direction across a basin for years, including below 2,000 metres and beneath ice. Capturing seasons and moving swirls would establish sustained coverage.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm map detail and accuracy
milestones.explanation: Independent observations would have to confirm all mapped quantities against numerical targets set beforehand for detail, timing, gaps and errors. This would establish that the maps resolve evolving structures.

milestones.label: Heat and freshwater estimates become more precise
milestones.explanation: Estimates of basin heat and freshwater storage and transport would have to reduce uncertainty against a defined current baseline, including boundary exchanges. This would demonstrate the scientific benefit.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and establish limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the main results using shared observations and methods across contrasting conditions, with operating needs and gaps stated. This would establish reliability within the tested conditions.

uncertain: The numerical targets for map detail, sampling frequency, errors and acceptable coverage gaps remain undefined.
The comparison system and the size of uncertainty reduction needed for success remain unspecified.
Sound speed alone cannot separate temperature from salt levels; whether combined observations can recover all requested quantities remains open.
